extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of physics and philosophy of science (advanced undergraduates/general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining operational definitions and conceptual foundations of mass, force, density, and the laws of motion, and discussing limits and assumptions of applying these laws across physical scales. Emphasizes measurement procedures (weighing), conceptual classification (density), and problems (aspect, modified action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conception of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass of A relative to a standard Q is defined by the ratio: Mass_of_A = (Acceleration of Q due to A) / (Acceleration of A due to Q). Mass is always a relative quantity and is a mere number representing a ratio of accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition makes mass an intelligible, operational concept determined scientifically by mutual accelerations relative to a chosen standard corpuscle Q. Text-book definitions of mass as 'the quantity of matter in a body' are criticized as idle (see footnote). If the standard Q is taken of unit mass (unity), formulas simplify accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual accelerations inversely as masses (Fifth law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the acceleration of A due to B to the acceleration of B due to A is exactly equal to the ratio of the mass of B to the mass of A — i.e. mutual accelerations are inversely as masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraically: (Acceleration of A due to B) / (Acceleration of B due to A) = Mass of B / Mass of A. From this follows that Mass_A * (acceleration of A due to B) = Mass_B * (acceleration of B due to A). This relation motivates the operational definition of force and underlies Newton's statement 'Action and Reaction are equal and opposite.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Force of B on A is defined as the product of the mass of A and the acceleration of A due to B (i.e. mass × acceleration). The direction and sense of this force are those of the acceleration of A due to B, and its magnitude is obtained by multiplying the numerical units of acceleration by the numerical units of mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force is therefore an arbitrary conceptual measure of motion (measured in units of mass-acceleration) without any direct perceptual equivalent. The text warns against ordinary text-book or metaphysical definitions that treat force as a 'cause' of motion; instead force is a shorthand, operational symbol chosen because of its convenience and general use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of masses tested by weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality of masses can be tested by an idealized weighing-machine: two particles A and B suspended from a weightless inextensible string placed over a perfectly smooth cylinder will balance (be at rest relative to the field) only if their masses are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When masses are equal (m_A = m_B), the tension in the string equals m_A * g (the weight). Hence if the local earth-acceleration g is known, mass can be measured in terms of tension. The derivation uses the combined-acceleration relations and yields explicit formulas for acceleration and string tension (equations (iii) and (iv) referenced in the text). Equality of strains/tensions is thus an experimental method for comparing masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density as the basis of the kinetic scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Density is defined kinetically as the ratio of the masses of infinitesimal equal volumes of a substance and of a chosen standard homogeneous substance; for homogeneous substances density is constant and proportional to mass per volume, while for heterogeneous substances density varies from point to point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density is the fundamental means of kinetically classifying particles and individualizing substances for the mechanical model: it links geometrical volume to the masses of conceptual particles and the accelerations assigned to them. The text emphasizes that homogeneity, equal volumes, and density-at-a-point are ideal/conceptual limits not exactly realizable in perception; density is a conceptual, not a strictly perceptual, notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of aspect on mutual accelerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether the absolute magnitudes of mutual accelerations of two corpuscles are influenced by the aspect (orientation/posture) they present to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The answer is unsettled: aspect likely plays little role for ether-elements, may be significant for prime-atoms depending on their internal model, and is probably an important factor for chemical atoms and molecules (and thus for phenomena like crystallization and magnetization). For gravitation, aspect shows no perceptible effect. Aspect should be considered a potentially significant factor when determining absolute mutual accelerations, especially at small scales or for structured bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis of modified action / superposition question
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining accelerations for synthesis of motion, ask: if the acceleration of A due to B is known, will that acceleration be altered when a third body C is introduced? Equivalently, are accelerations simply combinable (additive) when multiple sources are present?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the problem of modified action and is central to constructing motion of complex groups from simple pairs. The text frames the expectation (in some cases) that combined accelerations may be represented by the diagonal step given by combining rules (p. 282), but stresses this is a critical question — superposition cannot be assumed without justification and must be examined for the specific mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on applicability of particle laws across scales
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth and fifth laws of motion, and their associated definitions of mass and force, are established for particles but may not validly extend unchanged to ether-elements, prime-atoms, atoms, molecules, or interactions between ether and 'gross matter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must be cautious about dogmatically asserting that laws valid for particles apply across the conceptual model; structural differences (e.g., extended vs point-like constituents, internal motion) may alter how masses and mutual accelerations relate. The text advocates experimental investigation and imaginative theoretical development rather than uncritical extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific terminology should be operational and avoid metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: Science 'answers no why — it simply provides a shorthand description of the how of our sense-impressions.' Terms like mass and force should be used as conceptual symbols describing observable relations, not as metaphysical entities invoked to cloak ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions must be tied to measurable/operational relations (e.g., mutual accelerations, tension in a string) and one should resist projecting mental/conceptual constructs (like 'matter' as a source) into the perceptual field. If scientific terms are to be useful they must serve to describe 'how' phenomena occur rather than assert untestable 'why' explanations.
